questions.question: What is excluded by the word "nonconstant" in the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra?
options: Quadratic polynomials such as $z^2+1$.
Polynomials with complex coefficients.
Polynomials with repeated roots.
Constant polynomials such as $p(z)=5$.

questions.question: What does “counted with multiplicity” mean for roots?
options: Each distinct root is counted once, however often its factor repeats.
A root appearing as a repeated factor is counted more than once.
A real root is counted twice, to pair it with its conjugate.
Each root is counted as many times as the degree of the polynomial.

questions.question: Why is $x^2+1$ a motivating example rather than a counterexample?
options: Because it has the complex roots $\mathrm{i}$ and $-\mathrm{i}$.
Because it has the real roots $1$ and $-1$.
Because it is not a polynomial.
Because the theorem does not apply to quadratics.

questions.question: For $p(z)=(z-1)^2$, how many roots are counted with multiplicity?
Which roots does $z^2+1$ have in $\mathbb{C}$?
options: No roots in $\mathbb{C}$
$\mathrm{i}$ and $-\mathrm{i}$

questions.question: What is stronger: “at least one root” or “exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity”?
options: “Exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity” is stronger for degree $n\ge1$.
“At least one root” is stronger, because it is the theorem as first stated.
They are equivalent, since one root already fixes all $n$ roots.
Neither is stronger: they concern different sets of polynomials.

questions.question: What property of $\mathbb{C}$ is captured by the phrase “algebraically closed”?
options: Every nonconstant polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ has a real root.
Every nonconstant polynomial over $\mathbb{R}$ has a real root.
Every nonconstant polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ has a root.
Every convergent sequence in $\mathbb{C}$ has its limit in $\mathbb{C}$.

questions.question: For $p(z)=(z-2)^2(z+1)$, how many roots are counted with multiplicity?
Which factorisation over $\mathbb{C}$ matches $z^2+1$?
options: $(z-\mathrm{i})(z+\mathrm{i})$
It cannot be factored into linear factors over $\mathbb{C}$.

questions.question: A polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ has degree $4$ and roots $1,1,\mathrm{i},-\mathrm{i}$ counted with multiplicity. What can be said about its root count?
options: It has exactly the expected number of roots counted with multiplicity.
It has only three roots, since the repeated root $1$ is counted just once.
It violates the theorem because two roots are non-real.
It has the expected number of roots only if its coefficients are real.

questions.question: If a polynomial has real coefficients, what extra pattern may appear among its non-real roots beyond the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra?
options: Non-real roots occur in pairs $z$ and $-z$.
Non-real roots occur in reciprocal pairs $z$ and $1/z$.
Non-real roots are all purely imaginary.
Non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs.

questions.question: For $p(z)=(z^2+1)^2$, why do both roots have multiplicity $2$?
options: Because every non-real root automatically has multiplicity $2$.
Because $p(z)=(z-\mathrm{i})^2(z+\mathrm{i})^2$.
Because the polynomial has degree $4$, so each root must appear four times.
Because $z^2+1$ has no complex roots before squaring.

questions.question: A non-zero polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ has degree $5$. Three roots counted with multiplicity are known. What does the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra imply about the remaining count?
options: There can be no more roots.
There must be two more distinct real roots.
The polynomial must have degree $3$ instead.
Two roots remain over $\mathbb{C}$, with multiplicity.
